title: Assessment of risk factors of venous infarction in cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
content:
by Yasemin Dinç, Rıfat Ozpar, Deniz Sigirli, Emel Oguz Akarsu, Furkan Sarıdas, Cemile Haki, Suat Kamışlı, Bahattin Hakyemez

Introduction

Venous infarction is a frequent and severe complication of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) and is associated with poor clinical outcomes. However, the determinants of venous infarction remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify clinical and radiological risk factors associated with venous infarction in patients with CVST, with a particular focus on venous drainage patterns.

Methods

We retrospectively analysed 263 consecutive patients diagnosed with CVST at two tertiary referral centres between 01.06.2019 and 31.12.2024. Clinical characteristics, aetiological factors, and procedural histories were recorded. All patients underwent cranial MRI and MRI venography. Venous infarctions were classified as haemorrhagic or non-haemorrhagic. Venous collateral status was graded using a venous collateral scale (VCS). Cortical vein thrombosis (CoVT), thrombosed sinuses, and clinical outcomes at three months were assessed. Multivariable binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent risk factors for venous infarction.

Results

Venous infarction was detected in 93 patients. In multivariable analysis, puerperium, superior sagittal sinus thrombosis, poor venous collateralisation, and involvement of cortical vein thrombosis, were identified as independent risk factors for venous infarction. In contrast, thrombosis of transverse, sigmoid, and jugular veins, as well as the number of thrombosed venous structures, was not independently associated with venous infarction. Venous infarction was strongly associated with early neurological deterioration, radiological signs of mass effect, and poor functional outcome.

Conclusions

Poor venous collateralisation and cortical vein thrombosis were independently associated with venous infarction in patients with CVST. Assessment of cortical vein involvement and venous collateral status is essential for early risk stratification and clinical management of patients with CVST.
